analysis.investment_thesis: Central Bank of India is a government-owned PSU bank that was loss-making for six consecutive years (FY16–FY21) and has only recently turned modestly profitable; nine-year revenue CAGR of 3% and ROE of 11.4% on a bloated balance sheet offer no margin of safety for a long-term investor. PSU bank governance, chronic NPA cycles, and government capital allocation decisions make this permanently uninvestable for me.
key_strengths: Trading at 0.82x book — statistically cheap, and recent profit recovery to INR 3,943 Cr (FY25) shows the bad-loan cleanup is bearing some fruit
Government promoter at 89.27% guarantees it will never go bankrupt — a floor of sorts
Franchise of legacy branches provides a low-cost deposit base in semi-urban India
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of 3% over nine years in a period of strong credit growth means Central Bank has been consistently losing market share to private banks and better-run PSUs
OCF was positive only 1 out of 5 years — the bank is consuming rather than generating cash, and growing its balance sheet (assets up from INR 357K Cr to INR 505K Cr) on external funding
ROE of 11.4% after years of recapitalisation by the government is inadequate — shareholders are not being rewarded for the risk they carry
red_flags: Six years of consecutive net losses (FY16-FY21 totalling over INR 16,000 Cr in cumulative losses) — this is not a temporary blip but a structural failure of credit underwriting and governance
Government as 89% promoter means management quality, lending decisions, and capital allocation are all subject to political considerations — not commercial logic
Finance costs growing at 11.9% CAGR while total revenue grows at only 3% CAGR — the liability franchise is deteriorating in mix and cost relative to asset yields
analysis.detailed_analysis: I have watched PSU banks destroy shareholder capital for decades. Central Bank fits the pattern perfectly: years of NPA-driven losses, government bailouts, and then a cyclical profit recovery that markets celebrate. The current profitability is largely driven by NPA write-back tailwinds and a rising rate cycle — neither of which is durable moat-based earnings. When the credit cycle turns, these gains reverse quickly.
